260.title: Farid: the Creator in creation
260.hook: the Creator lives in creation and creation in the Creator, so whom can we call bad (Farid salok, ang 1381)
260.tomorrow: Farid: the crows and the eyes
260.howItsDone: Farid's salok on the Creator in creation is widely quoted by Sikhs, often with Kabir's 'from one light', to speak of seeing God in every person.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Farid on the blow you don't return: go home in peace. Today, the reason underneath it.

Anyone who's spent time around small children has heard the rule, or used it. Not: you're a bad boy. Instead: that was a bad thing to do. Teachers and parents swear by it, because a child who keeps hearing he is bad starts to believe it. Grown-ups break that rule about each other all day, mostly in their heads: that coworker is useless, that cousin is impossible. And once someone's filed under bad, you stop seeing anything else in them. Sheikh Farid, the Sufi of Pakpattan, asked a question that makes that filing system very hard to keep running.
screen: `NOT: YOU'RE A BAD KID.` → `THAT WAS A BAD THING TO DO.` → `FARID'S QUESTION.`

segments.voice: On Ang 1381 comes this salok: fareedaa khaalak khalak mahi khalak vasai rab maahi; mandaa kis no aakheeai jaa tis bin koee naahi. Farid, the Creator is in the creation, and the creation lives in God. Whom, then, can we call bad, when there's no one without Him? The first half should sound familiar. Six days ago, Kabir's hymn on Ang 1349 used the same pair of Arabic words: khaalik, the Creator, and khalak, the creation, each folded into the other. So it isn't a new idea; it's an older voice. Farid lived in the thirteenth century, about two hundred years before Kabir, and the Gurus kept both in one book. But Farid's question is narrower, and sharper. Kabir asked who is good and who is bad. Farid's verb is aakheeai, to call, to say out loud: not who is bad, but whom shall we call bad. It's a question about the tongue, the label hung on someone. You heard the same two words, mandaa and aakheeai, on day 247, when Guru Nanak asked why woman should be called lesser. Each time, the question turns back on the one doing the calling. Careful, though. Farid isn't saying nothing is ever wrong; his saloks are full of warnings about wasted lives and cruel deeds. You can name a wrong act clearly. What he questions is the word stamped on the whole person: bad, done, filed. That label fits no one, because there's no one without God in them. So the file never quite closes.
screen: `KHAALIK AND KHALAK, AGAIN.` · `FARID, TWO CENTURIES BEFORE KABIR.` · `AAKHEEAI — WHOM SHALL WE CALL BAD.` · `NAME THE DEED, NOT THE PERSON.` · then, large: `WHOM SHALL I CALL BAD.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind one person you've quietly filed under bad, without pretending they've done nothing wrong. Set Farid's question beside them: the Creator lives in them too, so whom shall I call bad? If nothing shifts, that's fine; just breathe with the question and let it stay open.
Farid. Here, his salok: the Creator is in the creation and the creation in God, so whom can we call bad, when no one is without Him?
Your line: whom shall I call bad. The deed can be named; the person stays open. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 260 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FARID: THE CROWS AND THE EYES.`

261.title: Farid: the crows and the eyes
261.hook: crows may peck the whole body, but spare the two eyes that hope to see the Beloved (Farid salok, ang 1382)
261.howItsDone: Farid's saloks of longing, including the crow couplet, are sung in Sikh kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Farid's question, whom shall I call bad, with the Creator living in everyone. Today, a couplet that starts with crows and ends in hope.

A porch light left on all night. A chair turned toward the road. Someone has waited so long for a person to come home that the tea went cold and meals were forgotten. Almost anything could go, except the view of the road, the one place the beloved would appear. Farid has a picture of that kind of waiting, and it's not gentle: a body, worn out, with crows landing on it. And one small, fierce request.
screen: `A LIGHT LEFT ON ALL NIGHT.` → `STILL WATCHING THE ROAD.` → `ONE THING NOT GIVEN UP.`

segments.voice: Near the end of his saloks, on Ang 1382, Farid paints himself as someone who has waited a whole life for God. In paraphrase: my body has dried to a skeleton, and crows peck at my palms; and still the Lord hasn't come. Look at the fate of this servant. Then the next salok, in the original: kaagaa karang dhandholiaa sagalaa khaaiaa maas; e due nainaa mat chhuhau pir dekhan kee aas. Crow, you've searched my skeleton and eaten all my flesh. But please don't touch these two eyes. I still hope to see my Beloved. Crows and a skeleton are shocking at first. But it's the bride and her longing again, birha, from day two hundred forty-five, told in a stark picture. Everything can go: comfort, youth, strength, the body itself. The one thing he asks to keep is the ability to look for the one he loves. Some readers hear more in the crows: all the things that pick at a life, worries, desires, the years, the world's small bites. Let them take what they take. Just keep the eyes, the part of you still turned toward God, or toward what's good, still hoping. Pir here means the beloved, the husband, and for Farid, God. Aas means hope. So the couplet ends not in despair but in hope, stubborn and alive, while there are still eyes to see.
screen: `A BODY WORN TO BONE.` · `KAAGAA — CROW, TAKE THE REST.` · `BUT SPARE THE TWO EYES.` · `AAS — HOPE TO SEE THE BELOVED.` · then, large: `SPARE THE EYES.`

segments.voice: If you can, look out a window or up at the sky; if not, close your eyes and picture it. Let the day's worries be the crows, pecking at what they like for a minute. Keep your gaze soft and open, with a little longing in it: for God, if you pray, or for goodness, peace, someone you love.
Farid. Here, his salok: crow, take my flesh, but spare these two eyes, for I still hope to see my Beloved.
Your line: spare the eyes. Whatever the day takes, the eyes that hope can stay. Day two hundred sixty-one, done.

262.title: The Gurus answer Farid
262.hook: Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan added their own saloks among Farid's, answering him gently
262.howItsDone: In the Guru Granth Sahib, each salok is marked with its author, so readers of Farid's saloks can see where Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan reply, and Sikh commentaries read them as a dialogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Farid's crows and his plea: spare the eyes, I still hope. Today, someone answers Farid, centuries after he spoke.

An old book, passed down in a family. In the margin, a grandfather once wrote: life is hard, I've wasted my years. Decades later, a grandchild wrote beside it: not wasted, it isn't too late. Two people, perhaps strangers, talking across the page. The Guru Granth Sahib has pages like that. Beside Farid's saloks sit a few short verses marked with the Gurus' names, and read together, they turn out to be replies.
screen: `AN OLD FAMILY BOOK.` → `NOTES IN THE MARGIN.` → `TWO PEOPLE, TALKING ACROSS TIME.`

segments.voice: Among Sheikh Farid's saloks, the Guru Granth Sahib sets a handful by the Gurus: Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan. Each is marked with its Mahala, so you always know who's speaking. Some pick up Farid's exact words and turn them, gently. Here are two, in paraphrase. Farid says: those who didn't love the Lord when their hair was black, hardly anyone manages it once the hair turns white. So love the Lord, and your color will be ever new. It sounds like a warning: you may already be too late. Guru Amar Das answers, starting with Farid's own name: Farid, black hair or white, the Lord is always there, if anyone remembers. And love like that isn't won by effort alone, however much we long; it comes as a gift, by grace. Not too late: the Lord is there at every age. Elsewhere Farid, in his longing, says: my body burns like an oven, my bones burn like firewood; if my feet grow tired, I'll walk on my head to meet my Beloved. Guru Nanak answers: don't heat your body like an oven, don't burn your bones. What have your head and feet done wrong? See your Beloved within. Listen to the tone. The Gurus don't mock Farid or correct him coldly. They honor his longing, then open a softer door. That's how the book is built: not one voice lecturing, but a conversation across centuries, held with respect.

segments.voice: Think of someone older than you, a parent, a grandparent, an old teacher, a neighbor, and something they often say that you see differently. Picture answering them the way the Gurus answered Farid: first honoring what's true in it, then offering your view softly, by name, with respect.

263.title: More Bhagats ahead
263.hook: Namdev, Ravidas, Dhanna, Sain and others wait for year three
263.howItsDone: The hymns of all the Bhagats are read and sung in Sikh worship alongside the Gurus', and communities such as the followers of Ravidas and Namdev especially cherish their hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mahala, the mark of which Guru is speaking, and the Gurus answering Farid across the centuries. Today, the last day with the Bhagats for now, and a look at who's still waiting.

The last guests are leaving a long dinner, and across the room there's a whole table of people nobody got to meet. Someone's laughing, someone's telling a story, and the thought is: next time. For twelve days this path has sat with two voices, Kabir and Farid. But the Guru's book has a much bigger table. Today, a first glimpse of the others.
screen: `THE END OF A DINNER PARTY.` → `A TABLE YOU NEVER MET.` → `NEXT TIME.`

segments.voice: Walk past that table and hear the names. Namdev, from Maharashtra, a calico printer; stories say he sang so lovingly that a temple turned toward him. Ravidas of Benares, a leatherworker from a caste many refused to touch; he sang of Begampura, a city without sorrow, where no one is second-class. Dhanna, a farmer from Rajasthan. Sain, a barber who, it's said, served at a king's court. Pipa, a king who, tradition says, gave up his throne to become a devotee. Trilochan, Beni, Jaidev, Bhikhan, Sadhna, Ramanand, Parmanand, Surdas. Hindus and Muslims, Brahmins and people shut out of temples, across several centuries and much of India. You'll meet them properly later on the path, in year three. For now, look back at twelve days with just two of them. Kabir the weaver, whose loom was a prayer. One light made all. The warrior who fights for the helpless. The death that delights. Short, sharp saloks. Farid of Pakpattan, speaking in his own Punjabi. Don't strike back. The Creator in creation. Spare the eyes. And the Gurus answering, gently, across the centuries. What they share is what the Gurus heard in them: one God, the Name, love over ritual, and no patience for the walls people build between each other. That's why their words sit in the Guru's book, and why the book still has more voices ahead.
screen: `NAMDEV, RAVIDAS, DHANNA, SAIN.` · `PIPA, JAIDEV, SADHNA, SURDAS…` · `TWELVE DAYS WITH KABIR AND FARID.` · `ONE GOD, THE NAME, NO WALLS.` · then, large: `MORE VOICES AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Pick one name you heard, Namdev, Ravidas, Dhanna, Sain, Pipa, any one, and say it aloud, softly, once. Think of what they were: a printer, a leatherworker, a farmer, a barber, a king. Let that name stand for everyone whose work the world overlooks, and whose voice was still kept.
Bhagat bani, the Bhagats' hymns. Namdev, Ravidas, Dhanna, Sain and others, whose hymns sit in the Guru Granth Sahib and wait for us later on the path.
Your line: more voices ahead. The table is bigger than it looks. Day two hundred sixty-three.

264.title: What rehat means
264.hook: rehat is the Sikh code of living, how the teaching becomes daily life
264.howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada, published by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, describes daily prayers (nitnem) in the morning, evening and at night, honest work, sharing and service; how closely each Sikh keeps it varies.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhagat bani: Namdev, Ravidas and more voices still ahead. Today, a new stretch, from the hymns to the way of life.

Before light, in a Sikh home, someone is already up. Washed, hair combed, a prayer said from memory in the half-dark. Later there's work, a meal shared with whoever is at the table, a prayer at evening and another before sleep. Ask which rule makes all that happen and the answer isn't one rule. It's a word for the whole shape of a day lived by the teaching: rehat.
screen: `BEFORE LIGHT, A PRAYER.` → `WORK, A SHARED MEAL, EVENING.` → `NOT ONE RULE: A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: The word is usually linked to the Punjabi rehna, to live, to stay, to dwell. So rehat is, at heart, a way of living: for Sikhs, the discipline that turns the Gurus' teaching into daily habit. Today the shared written reference is the Sikh Rehat Maryada, a short code agreed by Sikh leaders and scholars, which you'll look at closely in a few days. It holds much more than rules. It begins with who a Sikh is: someone who believes in one God, the ten Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib and the Gurus' teaching. Then the day: rising early, bathing, remembering the Name, reciting the set daily prayers, the nitnem, in the morning, the evening and before sleep. Then honest work, sharing, and serving others. Then life together: the gurdwara, the langar, the rites of birth, marriage and death. And for those who take amrit, the five Ks and a few things to avoid, which come over the next days. Here's the key. Rehat isn't meant as a checklist to earn God's favor; the Gurus were blunt that empty ritual saves no one. It's the shape a life takes when the teaching is actually lived: truth lived, from a couple of weeks ago. Sikhs also keep the rehat in very different degrees, and that's discussed honestly within the community. A way, not a list.
screen: `REHNA — TO LIVE, TO DWELL.` · `THE SIKH REHAT MARYADA.` · `THE DAY, THE WORK, THE SANGAT.` · `NOT A CHECKLIST: A LIVED SHAPE.` · then, large: `A WAY, NOT A LIST.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you always do, or never do, because of what you care about: maybe you don't lie to your kids, or you always call your mother, or you never eat in front of someone hungry. Put it into one short sentence, a rule you live by, and rest with the breath while you hold it.
Rehat. The Sikh way of living, from rehna, to live: the discipline that turns the Gurus' teaching into the shape of a day.
Your line: a way, not a list. It starts before light and ends after dark. Day two hundred sixty-four, done.

265.title: Kesh: hair as given
265.hook: uncut hair, kept as the Creator made it, and covered by the turban
265.howItsDone: Amritdhari Sikhs, and many other Sikhs, keep their hair uncut; many men and some women tie a turban (dastar) each day to cover it, while others cover it with a scarf (chunni).

segments.voice: Yesterday, rehat, the Sikh way of living: a way, not a list. Today, the first of the five Ks, and the most visible.

Haircuts, color, shaving, trimming, filters on every photo. So much of modern life is about changing how people look, and none of that is wrong. Now imagine choosing, for your whole life, to leave one thing exactly as it grew. Not as a style. As a promise. Millions of Sikhs do exactly that, and when you see a Sikh turban, you're seeing what it protects. Today, the first of the five articles of faith, the five Ks: kesh.
screen: `CUT, COLOR, SHAVE, FILTER.` → `ONE THING LEFT AS IT GREW.` → `NOT A STYLE: A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Kesh means hair, and in Sikh practice it means uncut hair, kept whole from head to toe, as the Creator made it. It's the first of the five Ks, the articles of faith that Sikh tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gave the Khalsa at Vaisakhi in 1699. All five begin with the sound k in Punjabi, which makes them easy to remember. Why keep the hair? Sikhs give several reasons, and they fit together. Acceptance: the body is the Creator's gift, and leaving it as made says, I accept the form I was given, in hukam, the order. Identity: the Gurus themselves kept their hair, and keeping it says, I stand with them, where anyone can see. Discipline: it can't come off for the weekend. A Sikh with uncut hair is recognizable on every street, and so accountable on every street. In a hymn of Guru Arjan, in paraphrase, a true Muslim is described as keeping the whole form intact, with a turban on the head, and Sikhs often cite the phrase saabat soorat, the whole, intact form, as part of their own ideal. The turban, the dastar, isn't one of the five Ks itself, but it protects and covers the kesh. Many Sikh men wear it, and some Sikh women do too; many more women cover their hair with a scarf, the chunni. Not every Sikh keeps uncut hair: many honor the Gurus while cutting it, and the community talks about that openly. For those who keep it, the promise is simple. As made.
screen: `KESH — HAIR, KEPT UNCUT.` · `THE FIRST OF THE FIVE KS, 1699.` · `ACCEPTANCE, IDENTITY, DISCIPLINE.` · `THE DASTAR COVERS AND PROTECTS.` · then, large: `AS MADE.`

segments.voice: If you can, move a brush, a comb or just your fingers slowly through your hair, as if it were a gift; if you have little or no hair, rest a hand gently on your head instead. Notice the body you were given, its shape, its warmth, the way it grew without your planning. For a moment, don't improve anything; let it be as made.
Kesh. Uncut hair, kept as the Creator made it and covered by the turban or a scarf; the first of the five Ks.
Your line: as made. The promise lives in what's left alone, just as it grew. See you tomorrow.

266.title: Kangha: the small comb
266.hook: a small wooden comb, for keeping the hair clean and ordered
266.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the five Ks wear a small comb, usually wooden, in their hair, and the Sikh Rehat Maryada asks them to comb the hair twice a day and tie the turban neatly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kesh: uncut hair, kept as made. Today, the second K, which lives right inside the first, and the end of a week.

Two gardens can grow from the same promise. In one, nothing is ever cut and nothing is ever tended: brambles everywhere, paths gone, beautiful in a wild way, but impossible to walk through. In the other, nothing has been cut either, but every morning the gardener walks through, untangles, clears the paths, sweeps. Same plants. Completely different garden. Uncut hair, in Sikh teaching, is meant to be the second garden. That's why, right in the kesh, Sikhs who keep the five Ks carry a small wooden comb.
screen: `TWO GARDENS, NOTHING CUT.` → `ONE WILD, ONE TENDED.` → `A COMB IN THE HAIR.`

segments.voice: Kangha means comb. It's the second of the five Ks: a small comb, usually wooden, kept in the hair, often tucked into the knot under the turban. Its job is plain: to keep the kesh clean and ordered. The Sikh Rehat Maryada asks Sikhs to comb their hair twice a day and tie the turban neatly. Why does such a small thing matter? Here's the usual explanation. In the Gurus' time, some ascetics wore their hair long and matted as a sign that they had left the world behind. The Sikh Gurus honored devotion, but they didn't ask anyone to leave the world. They taught householders to live in it: to work, marry, raise children, serve. So Sikhs keep their hair uncut, like the ascetics, and comb it, unlike the ascetics' matted locks. The kangha says: devotion inside ordinary life, not away from it. Some Sikhs also read it inwardly. Twice a day the comb pulls the tangles from the hair; twice a day the prayers do the same for the mind. Clean outside, ordered inside. And there's a gentleness in it. A comb doesn't cut anything or fight the hair. It just untangles, patiently, again tomorrow. That's the week, too: Farid's Creator in creation, the crows and the eyes, the Gurus answering Farid, the Bhagats still ahead, rehat, kesh, and now the kangha. The saints showed what to love. The rehat shows how to live it, morning and evening, one tangle at a time.
screen: `KANGHA — THE SMALL COMB.` · `COMB TWICE A DAY.` · `UNCUT, BUT NOT MATTED.` · `CLEAN OUTSIDE, ORDERED INSIDE.` · then, large: `CLEAN AND ORDERED.`

segments.voice: Picture tidying one small thing near you, a drawer, your desk, the kitchen counter, your phone's home screen, slowly, like a comb: nothing thrown out in a rush, just untangling and putting things back where they belong. Then turn that same gentle comb toward your mind, and let one tangled thought loosen.
Kangha. The small wooden comb kept in the hair, the second K, for keeping the kesh clean and ordered. This week: Farid twice, the Gurus' answers, more Bhagats, rehat, kesh, kangha.
Your line: clean and ordered. A comb never cuts; it only untangles. That's another week.

fork.setup: in the Gurus' time, some ascetics wore long, matted hair to show they'd left the world. what does the kangha say instead?
options: cut it all off.
keep the hair uncut, and keep it combed: devotion inside ordinary life.
leave it matted too.
fork.reveal: the Gurus taught householders to live in the world; uncut and tended, the hair says so every day.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kangha, comb; the second of the five Ks.

trapdoor: what you thought: a comb is just for grooming.
what it means: a sign that devotion belongs inside ordinary life, clean outside and ordered inside, one tangle at a time.

what a scholar hears: the kangha is usually explained against the matted locks (jata) of some ascetic orders; the Rehat Maryada's instruction to comb twice daily ties it to the morning and evening routine.
